# Modules, and what two days can produce
:::

::: {.hero-body}
A learning environment is far too much to build in a hackathon. It is also not a monolith. If you take
a process model of the course it has to support, the environment decomposes into modules with clear
inputs, outputs and interfaces — and then a small team can build *one* of them in two days without
waiting for the rest.

The decomposition below is taken from a process model of research-based learning developed at
Potsdam and implemented in the FL-Trail prototype
([Dehne 2021](https://doi.org/10.25932/publishup-49789)), which models self-organised learning as a
sequence of phases and identifies group formation, feedback, reflection and peer assessment as the
sub-processes worth supporting with software. The mapping onto self-regulated, project-based
**software engineering** teaching is nearly one-to-one, for a simple reason: an RSE course already
*is* a research project carried out in teams.

## The process model, mapped onto an RSE course

::: {.landscape .phases}

| Phase | In research-based learning | In a project-based RSE course | What software should do here |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 · Topic finding** | Formulating a question, or choosing one inside a set frame | Choosing the codebase, dataset, issue or method to work on | Nothing. Search engines and the instructor cover this; do not build it |
| **2 · Group formation** | Forming the research team | Forming the dev team | **The strongest case for software.** Group formation is an optimisation problem; an algorithm solves it without bias and at course scale, either homogeneously (by shared interest or learning goal) or heterogeneously (by complementary traits) |
| **3 · Concept design** | A dossier: question, state of the art, method, work plan | A design document: requirements, architecture sketch, test plan, data management, licence | Structured annotation of the document, plus an engine that decides *who reviews whom, and when*, so that every team is guaranteed feedback |
| **4 · Execution** | Carrying out the study | The sprint itself | Reflection anchored in the work — a learning log tied to commits and milestones — and the execution back-end the code runs on |
| **5 · Presentation** | Presenting results to peers | Demo, code walkthrough, release | Live presentation accompanied by structured peer assessment |
| **6 · Write-up** | The project report | README, documentation, a software paper | Nothing. This is Word, Quarto and Overleaf territory |
| **(Assessment)** | Peer review, grading | Peer code review, then a mark | A co-assessment procedure that lets learner judgements enter the grade in a defensible way |

:::

Two things follow that are easy to miss. First, software is worth building in **four** of the seven
rows, not all of them — a hackathon that starts by picking one of those four starts in the right
place. Second, review sits in two different places: in research, peer review comes in the
*middle* and gates the presentation; in teaching, grading traditionally comes at the *end*. An RSE
course wants both, and that is precisely what makes code review teachable — the same artefact is
reviewed formatively in phase 3–4 and assessed summatively at the end.

## Candidate modules for the two days

Each of these is a self-contained module with an interface an environment could call. None of them
requires the rest to exist first.

::: {.why-grid}

::: {.why-card}
### M1 · Group formation
Given participants and their interests, topics or self-reported strengths, return teams. Two
strategies, chosen by the instructor: homogeneous by shared learning goal, heterogeneous by
complementary profile — plus manual override, which must always remain available. A service with one
call, no UI needed, testable against synthetic cohorts of 200 in the room.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M2 · Artefact submission
In RSE the submitted artefact is a **repository at a commit**, not an uploaded file. A module that
takes a Git URL plus a ref, snapshots it, records the environment spec, and hands back a stable
identifier. Small, unglamorous, and everything downstream depends on it.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M3 · Peer code review
The assignment problem first — who reviews whose code, how many reviews each, ensuring nobody is
left without feedback — then a review surface with comments anchored to lines and to the rubric.
Forge review tools do the anchoring already; what they do not do is *assign* reviews pedagogically or
report back to a course.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M4 · Peer and co-assessment
A rubric plus an aggregation procedure that combines learner marks with the instructor mark into one
grade, with the weighting explicit and outliers visible. The hard part is not the interface, it is a
procedure teachers will actually stand behind in an exam board.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M5 · Reflection log
A lightweight portfolio bound to the work: reflection prompts triggered by commits, milestones or a
failed build, with tags tied to the learning goals of the course. This is where a run-of-the-mill
e-portfolio becomes RSE-specific — the log knows what the repository did.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M6 · Execution back-end
The piece nobody has: a defined contract for "run this learner artefact in this environment and
return the result" with one reference implementation — a container runner, JupyterHub or BinderHub —
and a clear statement of what it would take to put [SLURM]{.highlight} or Open OnDemand behind the
same interface.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### M7 · Module descriptor
One YAML file describing a teaching module: learning outcomes, prerequisites, languages, required
compute, licence, source repository. Effectively an RSE application profile of
[IEEE LOM]{.highlight}, cut down to what is actually known and actually used, with the fields that
learning technology never needed — hardware, toolchain, data.
:::

:::

If you want the shortest path to something demonstrable: **M1 → M2 → M3** is one coherent thin slice
of the learner loop — teams are formed, each team submits a repository, each team reviews the code of
another team — and it is the half of the loop that
[no existing platform closes](learning-environment.html), Gutenberg included.

## What the hackathon can realistically produce

Two days, a room of people who mostly have not worked together before, and no shared codebase at the
start. That rules a deployed platform out. It does not rule out artefacts that a follow-on project
can be built from — and for a proposal, a well-scoped set of these is worth more than a demo.

::: {.why-grid}

::: {.why-card}
### Certain
- A written requirements and landscape document: what exists, what is missing, what an RSE learning environment has to do
- A public repository with the design decisions recorded, issues filed and a roadmap
- A decision on build-on-Gutenberg versus build-new, with the reasoning written down
- A list of institutions and people willing to carry it on — the consortium for the next proposal
:::

::: {.why-card}
### Plausible
- **M7** as a draft schema, with two or three real modules described in it and validated by a script
- **M1** as a working service against a test cohort, since the algorithms are known and the problem is closed
- A specification of the review assignment in **M3**, and a prototype against mock data
:::

::: {.why-card}
### Not in two days
- A deployed, multi-tenant platform with real accounts
- Anything actually running on an HPC system, including allocations and identity
- A finished curriculum, or a complete set of modules
- A validated assessment procedure — validation takes a cohort and a semester, not a weekend
:::

:::

The honest framing is this: the hackathon produces a **specification, a thin slice and a
consortium**. The specification is what makes the follow-on fundable, the thin slice is what makes it
credible, and the consortium is what makes it happen.

## Pick a module before you arrive

Come with one of the seven in mind — or with a good argument that the decomposition is wrong.

[Register on Eventbrite](https://www.eventbrite.com/e/rse-hackathon-2026-at-university-of-glasgow-tickets-2000034040655){.cta target="_blank"}

Or join the [Matrix room](https://matrix.to/#/#rse-hackathon-glasgow-:matrix.org) first.

<button id="theme-toggle" class="theme-toggle" aria-label="Toggle light and dark mode">● Dark mode</button>
<script>
(function () {
  var root = document.documentElement;
  var btn = document.getElementById('theme-toggle');
  var stored = localStorage.getItem('theme-v2');
  function setDark() {
    root.setAttribute('data-theme', 'dark');
    btn.textContent = '☀ Light mode';
  }
  function setLight() {
    root.removeAttribute('data-theme');
    btn.textContent = '● Dark mode';
  }
  if (stored === 'dark') setDark();
  btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
    var isDark = root.getAttribute('data-theme') === 'dark';
    if (isDark) {
      setLight();
      localStorage.setItem('theme-v2', 'light');
    } else {
      setDark();
      localStorage.setItem('theme-v2', 'dark');
    }
  });
})();
</script>
